document.title: Wisconsin Standards for Science

BB9C653F32A64856920A392AD3C4D8F8.description: Students understand much of science deals with constructing explanations of how things change and how they remain stable. They quantify and model changes in systems over very short or very long periods of time. They see some changes are irreversible, and negative feedback can stabilize a system, while positive feedback can destabilize it. They recognize systems can be designed for greater or lesser stability.

0F124F304ADF4692B4ADE18590DCFA75.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and an understanding of stability and change to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

5A87A28D697C48D99058EDB4BCE3EDDF.description: Students investigate systems by examining the properties of different materials, the structures of different components, and their interconnections to reveal the system's function and solve a problem. They infer the functions and properties of natural and designed objects and systems from their overall structure, the way their components are shaped and used, and the molecular substructures of their various materials.

DB2C1B2E539E474E8C465792E91CC4F0.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and an understanding of structure and function to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

734983CF64F64B40AFAE5FD413BBD6F7.description: Students understand that the total amount of energy and matter in closed systems is conserved. They describe changes of energy and matter in a system in terms of energy and matter flows into, out of, and within that system. They also learn that energy cannot be created or destroyed. It only moves between one place and another place, between objects and/or fields, or between systems. Energy drives the cycling of matter within and between systems. In nuclear processes, atoms are not conserved, but the total number of protons plus neutrons is conserved.

83444750B1F245F2AC6F72D371035BD6.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and an understanding of energy and matter to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

1970B7C374D84A23A7157463061BDF12.description: Students investigate or analyze a system by defining its boundaries and initial conditions, as well as its inputs and outputs. They use models (e.g., physical, mathematical, computer models) to simulate the flow of energy, matter, and interactions within and between systems at different scales. They also use models and simulations to predict the behavior of a system, and recognize that these predictions have limited precision and reliability due to the assumptions and approximations inherent in the models. They also design systems to do specific tasks.

0B6704C83DD44AFC92FA6C209CACD60B.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and an understanding of systems and models to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

097678C5715A4595BD5BD542D1AB1FD0.description: Students understand the significance of a phenomenon is dependent on the scale, proportion, and quantity at which it occurs. They recognize patterns observable at one scale may not be observable or exist at other scales, and some systems can only be studied indirectly as they are too small, too large, too fast, or too slow to observe directly. They use orders of magnitude to understand how a model at one scale relates to a model at another scale. They use algebraic thinking to examine scientific data and predict the effect of a change in one variable on another (e.g., linear growth vs. exponential growth).

AA0832E3A6C74D1B95CAE05714E35D16.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and an understanding of scale, proportion and quantity to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

763171B8AEA84A7BB02B780488CAB7DE.description: Students understand empirical evidence is required to differentiate between cause and correlation and to make claims about specific causes and effects. They suggest cause and effect relationships to explain and predict behaviors in complex natural and designed systems. They also propose causal relationships by examining what is known about smaller scale mechanisms within the system. They recognize changes in systems may have various causes that may not have equal effects.

BD848E4DC84444A899E7288434F65059.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and cause and effect relationships to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

B968DCAF89B84E57856AA468E5AF90E4.description: Students observe patterns in systems at different scales and cite patterns as empirical evidence for causality in supporting their explanations of phenomena. They recognize classifications or explanations used at one scale may not be useful or need revision using a different scale, thus requiring improved investigations and experiments. They use mathematical representations to identify and analyze patterns of performance in order to reengineer a designed system.

932F067604254AD5B01E521608A7470D.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and patterns to make sense of phenomena and solve problem

8C26641764C7498B8E7EE32C742B6D6E.description: Communicate scientific and technical information in multiple formats, including orally, graphically, textually, and mathematically. Examples of information could include ideas about phenomena or the design and performance of a proposed process or system.

EA8D7867723D40208D332827EF159CDB.description: Synthesize and evaluate the validity and reliability of multiple claims, methods, or designs that appear in scientific and technical texts or media reports. Verify the data when possible.

E7431395A8FB4B39935A633FEF016F2A.description: Gather, read, and evaluate scientific and technical information from multiple authoritative sources, assessing the evidence and usefulness of each source.

F613050E595B4229BED38E69D4E1A8C6.description: Compare, integrate, and evaluate sources of information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively, or text-based) in order to address a scientific question or solve a problem.

BE138EF9B73649918D7B3224C76BAAED.description: Critically read scientific literature adapted for classroom use to determine the central ideas or conclusions, and to obtain scientific and technical information. Summarize complex evidence, concepts, processes, or information presented in a text by paraphrasing them in simpler but still accurate terms.

5AE8B9E795FF407DBAE90B2BAD51B4F4.description: Students evaluate the validity and reliability of claims, methods, and designs. This includes the following:

C6D3A745293247549F04392440A67084.description: Students will obtain, evaluate and communicate information, in conjunction with using crosscutting concepts and disciplinary core ideas, to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

E279CF153DB243E597EB245462E84B18.description: Evaluate competing design solutions to a real-world problem based on scientific ideas and principles, empirical evidence, and logical arguments. Consider relevant factors (e.g. economic, societal, environmental, and ethical considerations).

E81B250EE5A7497BB6B76EF9CF3C2029.description: Make and defend a claim based on evidence about the natural world or the effectiveness of a design solution that reflects scientific knowledge and student-generated evidence.

DCC275E5C2E940499FBF575395DE16E0.description: Construct, use, and present oral and written arguments or counter-arguments based on data and evidence.

9D37B65D3C4B4D24AF7BC6E218C9682D.description: Respectfully provide and receive critiques on scientific arguments by probing reasoning and evidence, by challenging ideas and conclusions, by responding thoughtfully to diverse perspectives, and by determining what additional information is required to resolve contradictions.

6CDAAA9917694E4E88BBC64D243AF7E9.description: Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning behind currently accepted explanations or solutions to determine the merits of arguments.

EAAEE50F3F6A4E1C91DC36EDB1D20202.description: Compare and evaluate competing arguments or design solutions in light of currently accepted explanations, new evidence, limitations (e.g., trade-offs), constraints, and ethical issues.

3D70B962661F4EE2BE12FFB4256455F9.description: Students use appropriate and sufficient evidence and scientific reasoning to defend and critique claims and explanations about the natural and designed world. Arguments may also come from current scientific or historical episodes in science. This includes the following:

831FEFF1B9F440638D2D090C161DE2C9.description: Students engage in argument from evidence, in conjunction with using crosscutting concepts and disciplinary core ideas, to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

56103A8830D94E59BBF1DEBD71E503F8.description: Consider trade-offs. Apply scientific ideas, principles, and evidence to solve design problems, taking into account possible unanticipated effects.

BB9C115D72F046C0B581A3461F822F00.description: Design, evaluate, and refine a solution to a complex real-world problem, based on scientific knowledge, student-generated sources of evidence, and prioritized criteria.

B0C903BE37DF42F6B8D205B3D89F8A01.description: Students create designs that are supported by multiple and independent student-generated sources of evidence consistent with scientific ideas, principles, and theories. This includes the following:

21FCFBF02AFF4897B01171A6921F717D.description: Apply scientific reasoning, theory, and models to link evidence to the claim and to assess the extent to which the reasoning and data support the explanation.

53BC3B4F78814F94A330CCFDC8302E14.description: Apply scientific ideas, principles, and evidence to provide an explanation of phenomena taking into account possible, unanticipated effects.

EA663108161B448292A3A6FB8194326A.description: Construct and revise an explanation based on valid and reliable evidence obtained from a variety of sources, including students' own investigations, models, theories, simulations, and peer review. Explanations should reflect the assumption that theories and laws that describe the natural world operate today as they did in the past and will continue to do so in the future.

0A6D8B071226460CA061FB6E3DC44C74.description: Make quantitative and qualitative claims regarding the relationship between dependent and independent variables.

96789F96AA4A4244AA433496A1A7B23B.description: Students create explanations that are supported by multiple and independent student-generated sources of evidence consistent with scientific ideas, principles, and theories. This includes the following:

6ABFDEDC16F1423AB7BB7E3B35A05A38.description: Students construct explanations and design solutions, in conjunction with using crosscutting concepts and disciplinary core ideas, to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

DCC3F0D9EA84423D99525B394FBCA165.description: Apply ratios, rates, percentages, and unit conversions in the context of complicated measurement problems involving quantities with derived or compound units (such as mg/mL, kg/m3, acre-feet, and others).

202906204D93471F8F6354FA1C3801EB.description: Use simple limit cases to test mathematical expressions, computer programs, algorithms, or simulations of a process or system to see if a model "makes sense" by comparing the outcomes with what is known about the real world.

89AA72FAADD24DDBB12835D28D5620F5.description: Apply techniques of algebra and functions to represent and solve scientific and engineering problems.

ED8DAE9FF94948AEB7864BE065A227B8.description: Use mathematical, computational, and algorithmic representations of phenomena or design solutions to describe and support claims and explanations.

9436FA6C92864999B74E26999A546AE7.description: Create and/or revise a computational model or simulation of a phenomenon, designed device, process, or system.

015C7241A2874FA59106E5BC93979B1F.description: Decide if qualitative or quantitative data are best to determine whether a proposed object or tool meets criteria for success.

95BFF2FA3C424CF0A718D72483661D1C.description: Students use algebraic thinking and analysis, a range of linear and nonlinear functions (including trigonometric functions, exponentials, and logarithms), and computational tools for statistical analysis to analyze, represent, and model data. Simple computational simulations are created and used based on mathematical models of basic assumptions. This includes the following:

DB5C9A599BC746159FFC8927D36E8653.description: Students use mathematics and computational thinking, in conjunction with using crosscutting concepts and disciplinary core ideas, to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

9D789F0CCCC4415890E027C3132CBF1B.description: Analyze data to optimize design features or characteristics of system components relative to criteria for success.

D18E4250A5EC4653B724D73FE4FB7C33.description: Evaluate the impact of new data on a working explanation or model of a proposed process or system.

DB69CDD47E26402986DE6C7E798A8682.description: Compare and contrast various types of data sets (e.g., self-generated, archival) to examine consistency of measurements and observations.

CB9A004CB5644848ABFCD7E4A3050C67.description: Consider and address more sophisticated limitations of data analysis (e.g., sample selection) when analyzing and interpreting data.

Consider possible variables or effects and evaluate the investigation's design to ensure variables are controlled.

BA4E2B64D9984D928FB06AA5B8E3FB80.description: Students use, synthesize, and develop models to predict and show relationships among variables and between systems and their components in the natural and designed world. This includes the following:

72E17559E5EF40C19348FD057FC11260.description: Clarify and refine an engineering problem.

8452A8565CEB488EAA0DC73E942CBC81.description: Define a design problem that involves the development of a process or system with interacting components and criteria and constraints that may include social, technical, and environmental considerations.

E5095129278A4D8AB038C542FEA3F33E.description: Ask questions that can be investigated within the scope of the school laboratory, research facilities, or field (e.g., outdoor environment) with available resources and, when appropriate, frame a hypothesis based on a model or theory.

E805E00B12B44DC79A27C6784348F717.description: Evaluate a question to determine if it is testable and relevant.

C6D630DBB7E64A999B60D1843A35D38A.description: Ask questions to clarify and refine a model or an explanation.

0038865880AA4D43817587BB89FBA352.description: Ask questions to determine relationships, including quantitative relationships, between independent and dependent variables.

3872A49EE5AC4444866F4A36B196BC0F.description: Ask questions that arise from examining models or theories to clarify and seek additional information and relationships.

3CDFEFE6B9944E4A9AFF0F05A5F408F4.description: Ask questions that arise from careful observation of phenomena, or unexpected results, to clarify and seek additional information.

BD206480E83E4AF6B919181750A67931.description: Students ask questions to formulate, refine, and evaluate empirically testable questions. This includes the following:

6CBE69107B9E41BAB0C5F454C3A44363.description: Students ask questions and define problems, in conjunction with using crosscutting concepts and disciplinary core ideas, to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

0177F600CB02438DA1EFB0475557EBF8.description: Engineers use a variety of approaches, tools, and techniques to define problems and develop solutions to those problems. Successful engineering solutions meet stakeholder needs and safety requirements, and are economically viable. Trade-offs in design aspects balance competing demands.

E5CAE0A1A65C4CB59A3E94D0E1A64231.description: The certainty and durability of science findings varies based on the strength of supporting evidence. Theories are usually modified if they are not able to accommodate new evidence.

83973D399AF24125AC5D8935693D1E87.description: Scientists use a variety of methods, tools and techniques to develop theories. A scientific theory is an explanation of some aspect of the natural word, based on evidence that has been repeatedly confirmed through observation, experimentation (hypothesis-testing), and peer review.

75D331978133463CB5DE459A213DA1AF.description: Science and Engineering Use Multiple Approaches to Create New Knowledge and Solve Problems

7807E67A10A84F69B03DF01ABCA01216.description: Science and engineering innovations may raise ethical issues for which science and engineering, by themselves, do not provide answers and solutions.

9CB6B01F1FF6402C9ED96923BB46A996.description: Science knowledge has a history that includes the refinement of, and changes to, theories, ideas and beliefs over time.

B89A94ADA3E5473BB6EDA43D1A9ACAC6.description: Science is both a body of knowledge that represents current understanding of natural systems and the processes used to refine, elaborate, revise and extend this knowledge. These processes differentiate science from other ways of knowing.

C7EC02B4B82041849A84582883CDEB2B.description: Science and Engineering Are Unique Ways of Thinking with Different Purposes

66684EC1AEB740DBB4F7A61ECAEBD008.description: Scientists and engineers embrace skepticism and critique as a community. Deliberate deceit in science is rare and is likely exposed through the peer review process. When discovered, intellectual dishonesty is condemned by the scientific community.

CDF2E6564A3E48E383688396204D9890.description: Some cultures have historically been marginalized in science and engineering discourse.

561B189CFC964D069A9907B754913064.description: Scientists' and engineers' backgrounds, perspectives, and fields of endeavor influence the nature of questions they ask, the definition of problems, and the nature of their findings and solutions.

F822BBC368A54AD4971DC579399C4965.description: Individuals from diverse backgrounds bring unique perspectives that are valuable to the outcomes and processes of science and engineering.

12CEDBFA45E04489B1153A8B52EBEEA0.description: Science and Engineering Are Human Endeavors

3D588F0923A14FD5AABA7FC0C89A5B2C.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of the nature of science and engineering to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

81893C3E515943E3B2D10C55F2AA135E.description: Analysis of costs and benefits is a critical aspect of decisions about technology.

81C8605C4AED40469831619ECC370A4F.description: New technologies can have deep impacts on society and the environment, including some that were not anticipated.

1EE2477524914C97BF0CFD08E345D6D9.description: Engineers continuously modify these systems to increase benefits while decreasing costs and risks.

A9032F956AA84E6082E83063A66EE48D.description: Modern civilization depends on major technological systems, such as agriculture, health, water, energy, transportation, manufacturing, construction, and communications.

AE5AF69D5FAE44698DD6850B8A600192.description: Influence of Engineering, Technology, and Science on Society and the Natural World

2906EB4BC0F441C0954D6A63A67A0D26.description: Many research and development projects may involve scientists, engineers, and others with wide ranges of expertise.

A67A7B98A3364DFAA8179B20A9A96144.description: Science and engineering complement each other in the cycle known as research and development (R&D).

483544FA3A0F41979DF69280FDE8258D.description: Interdependence of Science, Engineering, and Technology

A23219F5CD29436FB87BE9A0444F943E.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the links among Engineering, Technology, Science, and Society to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

98E1EABA22D34B6BAE1B35A65AFE5626.description: Criteria may need to be broken down into simpler ones that can be approached systematically, and decisions about the priority of certain criteria over others (trade-offs) may be needed.

249F5806F9F145799931EB127BFAF8EC.description: Both physical models and computers can be used in various ways to aid in the engineering design process. Computers are useful for a variety of purposes, such as running simulations to test different ways of solving a problem or to see which one is most efficient or economical. They are also useful in making a persuasive presentation to a client about how a given design will meet his or her needs.

4265487D8DE242F895D09C434B84AB45.description: When evaluating solutions, it is important to take into account a range of constraints, including cost, safety, reliability, and aesthetics, and to consider social, cultural, and environmental impacts.

3209B6C323CE46E7A6CF8017F39438E7.description: Humanity faces major global challenges today, such as the need for supplies of clean water and food or for energy sources that minimize pollution, which can be addressed through engineering. These global challenges also may have manifestations in local communities.

810BC72A090C4246ABA1C2BB58210778.description: Criteria and constraints also include satisfying any requirements set by society, such as taking issues of risk mitigation into account, and they should be quantified to the extent possible and stated in such a way that one can tell if a given design meets them.

B7FAEEBFBA484CC3A87BD3BE291FC18E.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of engineering design to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

0B01ED63BC934CA99E0133CF56B868E1.description: Engineering, Technology, and the Application of Science (ETS)

659EE4CA473B46A1B238032043739974.description: Global climate models used to predict changes continue to be improved, although discoveries about the global climate system are ongoing and continually needed.

5F1A2B0C9A4746D78E05E525DFC44696.description: Sustainability of human societies and the biodiversity that supports them requires responsible management of natural resources, including the development of technologies.

F00BDE2A539446D39DD1068B4340E85F.description: Natural hazards and other geological events have shaped the course of human history at local, regional, and global scales.

A2D45340ACCB4EBCB2E1BFFD524C4564.description: Resource availability has guided the development of human society and use of natural resources has associated costs, risks, and benefits.

1031554D508B4DEDA1FE1B6E6131CAE6.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the Earth and human activity to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

88E10040B3D347D4ABE3FD2D9D8267B3.description: The biosphere and Earth's other systems have many interconnections that cause a continual co-evolution of Earth's surface and life on it.

36E19BA283F04084BCBE64273B15088B.description: The role of radiation from the sun and its interactions with the atmosphere, ocean, and land are the foundation for the global climate system. Global climate models are used to predict future changes, including changes influenced by human behavior and natural factors.

D8A56C0C0DAC444DB7FCF748A735E255.description: The planet's dynamics are greatly influenced by water's unique chemical and physical properties

E79C14ED671B4A2ABE43DADD1ED85AC1.description: The Roles of Water in Earth's Surface Processes

25BE9D7DC4DA43C988BD26560A9A7435.description: Radioactive decay within Earth's interior contributes to thermal convection in the mantle.

3A4374C898764B7B870741651D41EBD2.description: Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System Interactions

6E94387E94B1455CBA72CA8E167E1A22.description: Feedback effects exist within and among Earth's systems.

074AB42230614346B7F2F193E811CD42.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of Earth's systems to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

FC8351F73BE04AA0AF53E46827A5D8DE.description: The rock record resulting from tectonic and other geoscience processes as well as objects from the solar system can provide evidence of Earth's early history and the relative ages of major geologic formations.

AF1643071F21403291725D38A10603D6.description: Kepler's laws describe common features of the motions of orbiting objects. Observations from astronomy and space probes provide evidence for explanations of solar system formation. Cyclical changes in Earth's tilt and orbit, occurring over tens to hundreds of thousands of years, cause cycles of ice ages and other gradual climate changes.

688454E6A22B4ED68B9197CC82BD3E73.description: Light spectra from stars are used to determine their characteristics, processes, and lifecycles. Solar activity creates the elements through nuclear fusion. The development of technologies has provided the astronomical data that provide the empirical evidence for the Big Bang theory.

BFB8497B8E0D4F108F9B751D103B7CB9.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of Earth's place in the universe to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

5CBA90986DB24103B95BD2E1F1C75BA6.description: Large amounts of information can be stored and shipped around as a result of being digitized.

2C6FC588613C4688986A49E66CD94325.description: Both an electromagnetic wave model and a photon model explain features of electromagnetic radiation broadly and describe common applications of electromagnetic radiation.

19EB599E4ACA4389A86B5B1F754B0061.description: The wavelength and frequency of a wave are related to one another by the speed of the wave, which depends on the type of wave and the medium through which it is passing. Waves can be used to transmit information and energy.

5A85E427B4B8424F9DB87D96BDDD9BCA.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of waves and their applications in technologies for information transfer to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

588E0695483447F7A5E788FC4606AE20.description: Photosynthesis is the primary biological means of capturing radiation from the sun; energy cannot be destroyed, but it can be converted to less useful forms.

C338B89452F240A8A1ACC6700483CA93.description: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

743663BF6BE84444B12A7CD61C01A951.description: Fields contain energy that depends on the arrangement of the objects in the field.

E978D0051F734DE2B2879E78ADBD815E.description: The total energy within a system is conserved. Energy transfer within and between systems can be described and predicted in terms of energy associated with the motion or configuration of particles (objects).

99510488526B440AA226DBA381124275.description: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

076E3B53099A4B4BB67AC1E47CC33472.description: Systems move towards more stable states.

5E964240DE5947A98F79535E80D6880D.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of energy to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

8DF792EE0685416A823AF566933970CE.description: Attraction and repulsion between electric charges at the atomic scale explain the structure, properties, and transformations of matter, as well as the contact forces between material objects.

C02CDB34C9CE4AD2B1FAE6D8E3938224.description: Forces at a distance are explained by fields that can transfer energy and can be described in terms of the arrangement and properties of the interacting objects and the distance between them. These forces can be used to describe the relationship between electrical and magnetic fields.

24DF9681E28343E7B76E1FFD70BB1045.description: If a system interacts with objects outside itself, the total momentum of the system can change; however, any such change is balanced by changes in the momentum of objects outside the system.

959652EBF2E54AC8A84CFA6C0213E397.description: Newton's second law of motion (F=ma) and the conservation of momentum can be used to predict changes in the motion of macroscopic objects.

1DFECF728AE440C58E863963396F4F07.description: Motion and changes in motion can be quantitatively described using concepts of speed, velocity, and acceleration (including speeding up, slowing down, and/or changing direction).

1D44D65A0843430A9EF24CD0CC2B35E4.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of forces, interactions, motion and stability to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

0BF3373A401B42EC9C9936785626D93A.description: Nuclear processes, including fusion, fission, and radioactive decays of unstable nuclei, involve release or absorption of energy.

B182DDD8585449BD8823FD7D7537DADD.description: Chemical processes are understood in terms of collisions of molecules, rearrangement of atoms, and changes in energy as determined by properties of elements involved.

6EAC678BE865484DA65EDE09668C846D.description: The sub-atomic structural model and interactions between electric charges at the atomic scale can be used to explain the structure and interactions of matter, including chemical reactions and nuclear processes. Repeating patterns of the periodic table reflect patterns of outer electrons. A stable molecule has less energy than the same set of atoms separated; one must provide at least this energy to take the molecule apart.

327854BC11B947D6A3CD58B46AD4FB52.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of matter and its interactions to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

EE4EEB36D65D42F3929E77259B406C5E.description: Biodiversity is increased by formation of new species and reduced by extinction. Humans depend on biodiversity but also have adverse impacts on it. Sustaining biodiversity is essential to supporting life on Earth.

5D28FC4E044B4957BFFB8DECD5E87522.description: Evolution results primarily from genetic variation of individuals in a species, competition for resources, and proliferation of organisms better able to survive and reproduce. Adaptation means that the distribution of traits in a population, as well as species expansion, emergence, or extinction, can change when conditions change.

5E1616C2B9814220995C012C90492175.description: Natural selection occurs only if there is variation in the genes and traits between organisms in a population. Traits that positively affect survival can become more common in a population.

41228852A0AE46CE805AE3AB7D3EAC0F.description: The ongoing branching that produces multiple lines of descent can be inferred by comparing DNA sequences, amino acid sequences, and anatomical and embryological evidence of different organisms.

659176781A9E488EAE0670AB2190C4DD.description: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

239E98B342EB4AC0A0F3C94A8E2A0389.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of biological evolution to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

FED491FD5CF84592A8745057D89EF519.description: The variation and distribution of traits in a population depend on genetic and environmental factors. Genetic variation can result from mutations caused by environmental factors or errors in DNA replication, or from chromosomes swapping sections during meiosis.

A512E2E17B3F4C3EAE217661A3256B6D.description: DNA carries instructions for forming species' characteristics. Each cell in an organism has the same genetic content, but genes expressed by cells can differ.

2D8AB56EE4774AA7933675BB235D214E.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of heredity to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

EBBB3D7E89F640A1902F6676E707386E.description: Group behavior has evolved because membership can increase the chances of survival for individuals and their genetic relatives.

EBB87EF894C54B70B1C3A2B4E88D0BA6.description: Photosynthesis and cellular respiration provide most of the energy for life processes. Only a fraction of matter consumed at the lower level of a food web is transferred up, resulting in fewer organisms at higher levels. At each link in an ecosystem, elements are combined in different ways, and matter and energy are conserved. Photosynthesis and cellular respiration are key components of the global carbon cycle.

25B880D30904419CA869A246DA4D5282.description: Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

F4E824E544E4450F872DBB4FB94357BB.description: Ecosystems have carrying capacities resulting from biotic and abiotic factors. The fundamental tension between resource availability and organism populations affects the abundance of species in any given ecosystem. The combination of the factors that affect an organism's success can be measured as a multidimensional niche.

FF3413585DD7465D922531BB80BBF2F6.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the interactions, energy, and dynamics within ecosystems to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

5AB59981C3C74C7799D294DC04287EE2.description: Organisms can process and store a variety of information through specific chemicals and interconnected networks.

86C617C532AF4E6989AA521D30292D49.description: The molecules produced through photosynthesis are used to make amino acids and other molecules that can be assembled into proteins or DNA. Through cellular respiration, matter and energy flow through different organizational levels of an organism as elements are recombined to form different products and transfer energy.

A835D71628584D23B56A8775E7287F7F.description: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

FFBED4C6F7F349EA959E090037DACB89.description: Growth and division of cells in organisms occurs by mitosis and differentiation for specific cell types.

699D325224FE4166B3071B570368B1B3.description: Systems of specialized cells within organisms help perform essential functions of life. Any one system in an organism is made up of numerous parts. Feedback mechanisms maintain an organism's internal conditions within certain limits and mediate behaviors.

31E42CDD0B794CC6A1BC0244A5EB038F.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of structures and processes (on a scale from molecules to organisms) to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

document.title: Wisconsin Standards for Science

79E4939B05F24A9B9778A5F56B912455.description: Obtain information using various texts, text features (e.g., headings, tables of contents, glossaries, electronic menus, icons), and other media that will be useful in answering scientific questions or supporting scientific claims.

544DD0D4B28A49EE91C287F146704A98.description: Students explain stability and change in natural or designed systems by examining changes over time, and considering forces at different scales, including the atomic scale. They design structures to serve particular functions by taking into account properties of different materials, and how materials can be shaped and used.

They also understand that within a natural or designed system the transfer of energy drives the motion and cycling of matter. Energy may take different forms (e.g. energy in fields, thermal energy, and energy of motion). The transfer of energy can be tracked as energy flows through a designed or natural system.

They also learn that models are limited in that they only represent certain aspects of the system under study.

They use proportional relationships (e.g., speed as the ratio of distance traveled to time taken) to gather information about the magnitude of properties and processes. They represent scientific relationships through the use of algebraic expressions and equations.

F0CEA80C2A534FE98B503A0084B39DAB.description: Ask questions to clarify or refine a model, an explanation, or an engineering problem.

1280F159FF284B27B3B6B10A7CB68810.description: Ask questions to identify and clarify evidence and the premise(s) of an argument.

6687656897514EB898DCA1B5BC104085.description: Ask questions that arise from careful observation of phenomena, models, or unexpected results, to clarify or seek additional information.

62844C6ABD644457ADAB9F7862855B93.description: Theories are explanations for observable phenomena based on a body of evidence developed over time. A hypothesis is a statement that can be tested to evaluate a theory. Scientific laws describe cause and effect relationships among observable phenomena.

26AA963842D24594BDDE06352832952F.description: A theory is an explanation of some aspect of the natural world. Scientists develop theories by using multiple approaches. Validity of these theories and explanations is increased through a peer review process that tests and evaluates the evidence supporting scientific claims.

45B4C6F513CD492784E8A5C5EDAFB789.description: Science and Engineering Use Multiple Approaches to Create New Knowledge and Solve Problems

3F6FFA8819AE4657ABB321C04580265C.description: Science and engineering have direct impacts on the quality of life for all people. Therefore, scientists and engineers need to pursue their work in an ethical manner that requires honesty, fairness and dedication to public health, safety and welfare.

F69413C39B444B97BC8F673DB5E57901.description: Engineering seeks solutions to human problems, including issues that arise due to human interaction with the environment. It uses some of the same practices as science and often applies scientific principles to solutions.

F4DF85CE02864E2C9F830923584245F6.description: Science asks questions to understand the natural world and assumes that objects and events in natural systems occur in consistent patterns that are understandable through measurement and observation. Science carefully considers and evaluates anomalies in data and evidence.

87D4DD897C7645899C7214887CCB262B.description: Science and Engineering Are Unique Ways of Thinking with Different Purposes

D7ECED088C084415BB745251E86BDABF.description: Science and engineering are influenced by what is valued in society.

BC161A2C06D240CD801DCA6CB8839B42.description: Scientists and engineers are persistent, use creativity, reasoning, and skepticism, and remain open to new ideas.

F8876136854C4E9E9BEB669CA708D90F.description: Individuals and teams from many nations, cultures and backgrounds have contributed to advances in science and engineering.

80B8C829F2DE49028CF96323D4C64CE5.description: Science and Engineering Are Human Endeavors

6214EDDFB04A453EAD574D202D0F8659.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of the nature of science and engineering to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

167C53BEE2AB4536AE691A11511B926B.description: Technology use varies over time and from region to region.

5526595BD01545578C33CA44DF944344.description: The uses of technologies are driven by people's needs, desires, and values; by the findings of scientific research; and by differences in such factors as climate, natural resources, and economic conditions.

37C8A5B3AC7D4F2E9944F260811DD715.description: All human activity draws on natural resources and has both short and long-term consequences, positive as well as negative, for the health of people and the natural environment.

3C2FD43A604441F8AB1A8871E7901D2C.description: Influence of Engineering, Technology, and Science on Society and the Natural World

DC1B71E5BA9541B58549AA7E8DE2685A.description: Science and technology drive each other forward.

8D9EA95D7DF64989A2974A514D40A95E.description: Engineering advances have led to important discoveries in virtually every field of science, and scientific discoveries have led to the development of entire industries and engineered systems.

6D6E7084E1684F9FBA0034CE3A61D921.description: Interdependence of Science, Engineering, and Technology

862E00DD97F04BEF817D356E0816837C.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the links among Engineering, Technology, Science, and Society to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

9EFE94E2DE014831ADFCECF116A53588.description: The iterative process of testing the most promising solutions and modifying what is proposed on the basis of the test results leads to greater refinement and ultimately to an optimal solution.

ACE32F68F1BE44C5ACECC9EE50350610.description: Although one design may not perform the best across all tests, identifying the characteristics of the design that performed the best in each test can provide useful information for the redesign process—That is, some of those characteristics may be incorporated into the new design.

365285AAA6B34066A0DDC2A04339E632.description: Models of all kinds are important for testing solutions.

41F28E9428C7448AABB0D66AF0EBFFCE.description: Sometimes parts of different solutions can be combined to create a solution that is better than any of its predecessors.

2BFC9C1A8AF04B7CBDDE47BC6A8FA487.description: A solution needs to be tested and then modified on the basis of the test results in order to improve it. There are systematic processes for evaluating solutions with respect to how well they meet the criteria and constraints of a problem.

CDABAA8C62304F5ABA3BC52B82DE950D.description: The more precisely a design task's criteria and constraints can be defined, the more likely it is that the designed solution will be successful. Specification of constraints includes consideration of scientific principles and other relevant knowledge that are likely to limit possible solutions.

9DD19F48AE4E43729FF7C5A6FB31BADE.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of engineering design to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

594EEB7F44AD4672A5E8F4A58556DF54.description: Engineering, Technology, and the Application of Science (ETS)

E2ED53E393F94EDDAD67F8C02F88B76E.description: Evidence suggests human activities affect global warming. Decisions to reduce the impact of global warming depend on understanding climate science, engineering capabilities, and social dynamics.

9BB7B455A7CC4E038FBC89374CDB47BC.description: Human activities have altered the hydrosphere, atmosphere, and lithosphere which in turn has altered the biosphere. Changes to the biosphere can have different impacts for different living things. Activities and technologies can be engineered to reduce people's impacts on Earth.

87244CF8B6864EB2967DE4F1F0A6A3B8.description: Patterns can be seen through mapping the history of natural hazards in a region and understanding related geological forces.

2DD07D4E68434A33B030F565E857640F.description: Humans depend on Earth's land, oceans, fresh water, atmosphere, and biosphere for different resources, many of which are limited or not renewable. Resources are distributed unevenly around the planet as a result of past geologic processes.

0E29F781B3B447F78C94B287833F4591.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the Earth and human activity to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

0B816F3E7DB54E02B6225EB4B0BDFDBE.description: The fossil record documents the existence, diversity, extinction, and change of many life forms throughout history.

5860138E44094705B96D936B9D249212.description: Complex interactions determine local weather patterns and influence climate, including the role of the ocean.

C6F5D5661A554505B530E3698D66EFF2.description: Water cycles among land, ocean, and atmosphere, and is propelled by sunlight and gravity. Density variations of sea water drive interconnected ocean currents. Water movement causes weathering and erosion, changing landscape features.

3D3E32C8C7E14B2B8F9CBC4875B9BFD2.description: The Roles of Water in Earth's Surface Processes

6669AE1171824609A8B2F5712829977D.description: Plate tectonics is the unifying theory that explains movements of rocks at Earth's surface and geological history. Maps are used to display evidence of plate movement.

AD9BDF23B8E449B9B4EDB04C82CAFA44.description: Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System Interactions

F8AF2B6739474DB396BF435918F98D4D.description: Energy flows and matter cycles within and among Earth's systems, including the sun and Earth's interior as primary energy sources. Plate tectonics is one result of these processes.

8035F4A814D34258A21D1A893ADE3552.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of Earth's systems to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

1B3841EFA02C4A2E865BE9B98DE4210C.description: Rock strata and the fossil record can be used as evidence to organize the relative occurrence of major historical events in Earth's history.

1F9A851AA5084DF5BAEF9440D96E4682.description: The solar system contains many varied objects held together by gravity. Solar system models explain and predict eclipses, lunar phases, and seasons.

0E8CA6E54A2D44D4A8C9C946C14A67F4.description: The solar system is part of the Milky Way, which is one of many billions of galaxies.

DD791C638F8C4EA698DAF23F619896A6.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of Earth's place in the universe to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

AFA9A678BDC347EFA819D704CE05D0C9.description: Waves can be used to transmit digital information. Digitized information is comprised of a pattern of 1s and 0s.

7693FFF7E85B4CEA85DE7BBE37CE45A3.description: The construct of a wave is used to model how light interacts with objects.

DAF043D5CFFC418B9E6A902200057DFE.description: A simple wave model has a repeating pattern with a specific wavelength, frequency, and amplitude, and mechanical waves need a medium through which they are transmitted. This model can explain many phenomena including sound and light. Waves can transmit energy.

D7195F2B66914BB99F0AEC348EFB8973.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of waves and their applications in technologies for information transfer to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

972A3F03D1D5400E9974FC7A4D525839.description: Sunlight is captured by plants and used in a chemical reaction to produce sugar molecules for storing this energy. This stored energy can be released by respiration or combustion, which can be reversed by burning those molecules to release energy.

C2AC6A922C544E4CB6D36557E5D2CB3D.description: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

A457DE8B46854649A42B06697364E791.description: When two objects interact, each one exerts a force on the other, and these forces can transfer energy between the interacting objects.

9BD8C0EA232D4902BA1B4F53AD676A82.description: Energy changes to and from each type can be tracked through physical or chemical interactions. The relationship between the temperature and the total energy of a system depends on the types, states, and amounts of matter.

3B5DE62A0A404246BB1746CA4926C8BB.description: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

18B3004EC3C94AEEAEC226DA1275677F.description: Kinetic energy can be distinguished from the various forms of potential energy.

089835934AE74C7EB89D9000C8704D07.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of energy to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

C05AA078A99F43E9BCBC9A2C0CB7D29E.description: Forces that act at a distance involve fields that can be mapped by their relative strength and effect on an object

FEF4E5F150384849A94C49000834DD6C.description: For any pair of interacting objects, the force exerted by the first object on the second object is equal in strength to the force that the second object exerts on the first, but in the opposite direction (Newton's third law).

25057280EF9A48739396226A6A18E837.description: The role of the mass of an object must be qualitatively accounted for in any change of motion due to the application of a force (Newton's first and second law).

569C605BE7514AB2BCBFCE3C12E64FD8.description: Motion and changes in motion can be qualitatively described using concepts of speed, velocity, and acceleration (including speeding up, slowing down, and/or changing direction).

94DF8DB5B2644D67B91FA063A01574C9.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of forces, interactions, motion and stability to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

DFF0398482FD4D4FB7564E717D60A026.description: Reacting substances rearrange to form different molecules, but the number of atoms is conserved. Some reactions release energy and others absorb energy.

5CAE67545C624A40B0098045B3836663.description: The fact that matter is composed of atoms and molecules can be used to explain the properties of substances, diversity of materials, states of matter, phase changes, and conservation of matter.

E0B007C3A3574613A125C0E21524931F.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of matter and its interactions to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

919CFCC2A32B4576B5C8E53DEC9AEA2F.description: Both natural and artificial selection result from certain traits giving some individuals an advantage in surviving and reproducing, leading to predominance of certain traits in a population.

6D23B662DBC740939F2C264C5B5B04A4.description: The fossil record documents the existence, diversity, extinction, and change of many life forms and their environments through Earth's history. The fossil record and comparisons of anatomical similarities between organisms enables the inference of lines of evolutionary descent.

1A60B337709C41338C4D4FF997F8B1E7.description: Evidence of Common Ancestry and Diversity

CFD49A1A72F3497CAAF9D88F7A14BD6D.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of biological evolution to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

73472F38FCB246688AC5606BCC1E0BD0.description: In sexual reproduction, each parent contributes half of the genes acquired by the offspring resulting in variation between parent and offspring. Genetic information can be altered because of mutations, which may result in beneficial, negative, or no change to proteins in or traits of an organism.

6A4CF88B935746DF96174080F6693B22.description: Genes chiefly regulate a specific protein, which affect an individual's traits.

3ECBBC00FEB742ED9BC9B29DB77D0E85.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of heredity to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

E29B49B9E0BE4E0DAED1039DCD099F35.description: Changes in biodiversity can influence humans' resources, such as food, energy, and medicines, as well as ecosystem services that humans rely on -- for example, water purification and recycling.

F417E89B619946C6ACE7589522582C8C.description: Ecosystem characteristics vary over time. Disruptions to any part of an ecosystem can lead to shifts in all of its populations. The completeness or integrity of an ecosystem's biodiversity is often used as a measure of its health.

FF909B932B4447A79308988BD8449C7C.description: The atoms that make up the organisms in an ecosystem are cycled repeatedly between the living and nonliving parts of the ecosystem. Food webs model how matter and energy are transferred among producers, consumers, and decomposers as the three groups interact within an ecosystem.

E0985033802B4A1087EC6F0C6A244B92.description: Cycles of Matter and Energy Transfer in Ecosystems

14762F785AFD494E9F50AD78956339E7.description: Organisms and populations are dependent on their environmental interactions both with other living things and with nonliving factors, any of which can limit their growth. Competitive, predatory, and mutually beneficial interactions vary across ecosystems but the patterns are shared.

671279E533C54E02A4D881F92337540B.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the interactions, energy, and dynamics within ecosystems to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

46BD0A82F8D44E438D4CFAB9645BFC5B.description: Plants use the energy from light to make sugars through photosynthesis. Within individual organisms, food is broken down through a series of chemical reactions that rearrange molecules and release energy.

A7821ABFFEB7444584D6CD8E1122B095.description: Organization for Matter and Energy Flow in Organisms

CE0776F6C4CC48A1A0E5F02E7FE21D2D.description: Animals engage in behaviors that increase the odds of reproduction. An organism's growth is affected by both genetic and environmental factors.

94D9700A395746038F85643DEBA5D85F.description: All living things are made up of cells. In organisms, cells work together to form tissues and organs that are specialized for particular body functions.

C1644A546B194EE588E3BDF56EE944DF.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of structures and processes (on a scale from molecules to organisms) to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

document.title: Wisconsin Standards for Science

AB413389EFB04FCF98F540B28C422BB2.description: Students use science and engineering practices, disciplinary core ideas, and an understanding of structure and function to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

5A7A3E58528546DB83429A7E627AA4DE.description: There is no perfect design in engineering. Designs that are best in some ways (e.g. safety or ease of use) may be inferior in other ways (e.g. cost or aesthetics).

F8417242DD584D26AF4B1A8A1E3015E2.description: The products of science and engineering are not developed through one set "scientific method" or "engineering design process." Instead, they use a variety of approaches described in the Science and Engineering Practices.

6B47FCA3B48C4F018E715EA2D5E5E5E5.description: Engineering solutions often have drawbacks as well as benefits.

F6D1FDB85DD24BDF8CFFF92B862672E4.description: Scientific findings are limited to what can be supported with evidence from the natural world. Basic laws of nature are the same everywhere in the universe (e.g. gravity, conservation of matter, energy transfer, etc.).

2D0A5561148F48B7A1B75CA0530C4736.description: Science and engineering are both bodies of knowledge and processes that add new knowledge to our understanding.

3CAB4E311A174E4AAF4017EF0AC60C6E.description: Science and Engineering Are Unique Ways of Thinking with Different Purposes

AADEDEACB76048AEA89A679892FA3940.description: Science and engineering affect everyday life.

D7472167331A4D548FA579FA3665F99F.description: People use the tools and practices of science and engineering in many different situations (e.g. land managers, technicians, nurses and welders).

396932031AB14E7791A842A61D24CBE6.description: Science and engineering knowledge have been created by many cultures.

0A7DC9CD0FCA4DD8977D9E4C9B43C44A.description: Science and Engineering Are Human Endeavors

B302B161D4414532BB6401E8DCF4A870.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of the nature of science and engineering to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

3AE9FF656ED445B3AA66038AABB4CAA9.description: When new technologies become available, they can bring about changes in the way people live and interact with one another.

F4DB30A17D1D43E291E6BCDF4D5C8D05.description: Engineers improve existing technologies or develop new ones to increase their benefits, decrease known risks, and meet societal demands.

53E75B1A549F4E5C85C4EA3801E32C62.description: People's needs and wants change over time, as do their demands for new and improved technologies.

F75E23B659204EA4A50F011FD31563E5.description: Influence of Engineering, Technology, and Science on Society and the Natural World

F1A4D414A1544F37AE69287841B4A514.description: Tools and instruments are used to answer scientific questions, while scientific discoveries lead to the development of new technologies.

4C72D94927A149ED8DB44BE9999AD9C3.description: Science and technology support each other.

C6BC62257FF249CA8E83A3D61FE68D05.description: Interdependence of Science, Engineering, and Technology

539B0FF6A3194FDE8CD5BA92A9100FA7.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the links among Engineering, Technology, Science, and Society to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

B62AA0A853D94F3A978DB394D9477693.description: Different solutions need to be tested in order to determine which of them best solves the problem, given the criteria and the constraints.

3C1523D18E3F42A98F780D4860F28761.description: Tests are often designed to identify failure points or difficulties, which suggest the elements of the design that need to be improved.

3534152085C244BFA3116C262C97A96A.description: At whatever stage, communicating with peers about proposed solutions is an important part of the design process, and shared ideas can lead to improved designs.

209C0804BF3748B884B720142FD9F8E5.description: Research on a problem should be carried out before beginning to design a solution. Testing a solution involves investigating how well it performs under a range of likely conditions.

CF1F772DB1554990960F6555F91A81D3.description: Possible solutions to a problem are limited by available materials and resources (constraints). The success of a designed solution is determined by considering the desired features of a solution (criteria). Different proposals for solutions can be compared on the basis of how well each one meets the specified criteria for success or how well each takes the constraints into account.

12BB4AE62BDB4BBC980EABED7FA24095.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of engineering design to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

0B4E526A63934023A7B667DE0317E51E.description: Engineering, Technology, and the Application of Science (ETS)

A89962B830D24B08B48381794654743A.description: Societal activities have had major effects on the land, ocean, atmosphere, and even outer space. Societal activities can also help protect Earth's resources and environments.

F1AA895C3EB44EAFAADBC832E0B99975.description: A variety of hazards result from natural processes; humans cannot eliminate hazards but can reduce their impacts.

0FC2296F2E224C91BCC9FC0AB5BB380E.description: Energy and fuels humans use are derived from natural sources, and their use affects the environment. Some resources are renewable over time, others are not.

D6E85735668143818E575CC15FB72782.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of the Earth and human activity to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

A0030049BE074D8580C8F47C68D0DE05.description: Living things can affect the physical characteristics of their environment.

A0FC9403E6F842B4ADA43B8A1929E807.description: Climate describes patterns of typical weather conditions over different scales and variations. Historical weather patterns can be analyzed.

84F25E4183A3466BAE34894FF51A1012.description: Most of Earth's water is in the ocean, and much of the Earth's freshwater is in glaciers or underground.

1076B0FD0C234190872C0E2685F58CC8.description: The Roles of Water in Earth's Surface Processes

AA06BD86831B4EE698846D62382BA006.description: Earth's physical features occur in patterns, as do earthquakes and volcanoes. Maps can be used to locate features and determine patterns in those events.

D99548C0170E4D529E45ADE51695C69E.description: Plate Tectonics and Large-Scale System Interactions

C9AC06D606F448E2B63E128F39BA60DC.description: Four major Earth systems interact. Rainfall helps to shape the land and affects the types of living things found in a region. Water, ice, wind, organisms, and gravity break rocks, soils, and sediments into smaller pieces and move them around.

FB46068C7C1F43A294705E007C0C5541.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of Earth's systems to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

D1A6256366D54BFB8E444201C8FDED66.description: Certain features on Earth can be used to order events that have occurred in a landscape.

63BD0538483F4B3A9AC5045870BA1D78.description: The Earth's orbit and rotation, and the orbit of the moon around the Earth cause observable patterns.

1057F61D70634540A2A122F8D615BD70.description: Stars range greatly in size and distance from Earth, and this can explain their relative brightness.

8F1D5744FDD2465C848BF1F49BE194DB.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of Earth's place in the universe to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

F960AE6BAB87439EBF35D9F4627C057F.description: Patterns can encode, send, receive, and decode information.

61F7CBBE20E34BDCA77645CF62CC7F86.description: Objects can be seen when light reflected from their surface enters our eyes.

3C1F6A94C7BE44EDBCD0E848E1CAAB03.description: Waves are regular patterns of motion, which can be made in water by disturbing the surface. Waves of the same type can differ in amplitude and wavelength. Waves can make objects move.

77081C70A13F417D9B18C90B70CBC94D.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of waves and their applications in technologies for information transfer to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

1D987D050FFA4100BED6661919877C57.description: Stored energy in food or fuel can be converted to useable energy.

B91D2A89232E450FB93E08823E516D88.description: Plants capture energy from sunlight which can be used as fuel or food.

7600B58265C1484EAEB4C20CA32E3E7B.description: Energy in Chemical Processes and Everyday Life

A93296C0B18C40F5A67F0CC4C9B2CFF5.description: When objects collide, contact forces transfer energy so as to change objects' motions.

67CB04D155FD447DA472C8B8F381FC44.description: Energy can be moved from place to place by moving objects, or through sound, light, or electrical currents. Energy can be converted from one form to another form.

F8CEFDBFD99A401E9C3C091D58F80897.description: Conservation of Energy and Energy Transfer

5075A5DD119743EE8C18633CF01346CE.description: Moving objects contain energy. The faster the object moves, the more energy it has.

9C4C28979DAE43B8BE0E64CA678B5BFE.description: Students use science and engineering practices, cross-cutting concepts, and an understanding of energy to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

653031DD89774369913B72263A7AE830.description: The gravitational force of Earth acting on an object near Earth's surface pulls that object toward the planet's center.

18D56E0BAFFB459CA5DE39AD689F64ED.description: Some forces act through contact, some forces (e.g. magnetic, electrostatic) act even when the objects are not in contact.

FE8F0759A79540078A3E715914745657.description: Patterns of motion can be used to predict future motion.

0A03922F2E114A1CB1459F00D9D0DEC1.description: The effect of unbalanced forces on an object results in a change of motion.

94CE2EDDC10541179E4D72F6732B7DC4.description: Qualities of motion and changes in motion require description of both size and direction.

45A727BF7FDF4C319F7973923BDB5EA6.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of forces, interactions, motion and stability to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

D7D3EFB55BB94568A99BD7A62836D324.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of matter and its interactions to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.

FB7BBD11526A48E0BCD3543EDEC307A1.description: Particular organisms can only survive in particular environments.

202EA372B30E41CD8BD6977D173C4A6A.description: Differences in characteristics between individuals of the same species provide advantages in surviving and reproducing.

48EC077850C040099364DA6C26498177.description: Food provides animals with the materials and energy they need for body repair, growth, warmth, and motion. Plants acquire material for growth chiefly from air, water, and process matter, and obtain energy from sunlight, which is used to maintain conditions necessary for survival.

E6F5244A9DC2433FB77BD60E7D42D54B.description: Students use science and engineering practices, crosscutting concepts, and an understanding of structures and processes (on a scale from molecules to organisms) to make sense of phenomena and solve problems.
